subject: gingerbreadHouse
pitch:
Category: Diorama.
Subject: gingerbread house.
Style: candy and icing.
reasoning:
I'm planning a static gingerbread house diorama model, keeping the design manageable at around 500-700 lines without joints, with geometry built directly in model space at a small scale of roughly 0.4 meters wide.

I'm sketching the layout: a cake board base with snow icing, a gingerbread-brown house body with a front facing outward, tilted roof slabs with candy tile rows, and white icing trim details, building each piece as separate parts using box and simple geometries with paint for grain and color variation.

Now I'm detailing the smaller features—an arched candy-bar door with a gumdrop knob and candy cane columns, glowing windows with cross-barred panes, a stacked chimney with icing top and swirled smoke, and striped candy cane posts using a sweep path with diagonal paint stripes.

I'm also planning gumdrops as flat-bottomed hemispheres with speckled sugar texture scattered around the base, lollipop and cone-shaped trees with frosted swirls and sprinkles, and a cute gingerbread man figure with iced face and buttons placed near the door.

I want a stepping-stone path of flattened candy discs leading to the door, a fence made of peppermint stick posts with an icing rail, snowy icing drifts along the roof ridge, and a swirled red-and-white peppermint decal on the front gable like a rose window.

Roof tiles will be rows of overlapping scalloped candy discs rotated to the roof plane, alternating through a small deterministic color palette, with icing-bead garlands along the eaves and scalloped icing swags draped along the front wall top. I'm also planning a set of 5-12 textures (window glow, door, peppermint, lollipop swirl, gingerbread face details built from small parts like eye spheres and gumdrop buttons) plus sugar crystal detailing.

I'm narrowing the texture list to around six: window, door, peppermint, two lollipop color variants, and a heart or snowflake accent, while handling wall decoration through zigzag icing trim sweeps rather than a separate SVG texture. Now I'm setting up the coordinate scheme—house centered at origin, board top at 0.02, snow mound surface at 0.03, and house base sitting at 0.03 to sink slightly into the snow.

Working out the house geometry: width 0.30, depth 0.22, wall height 0.15, with the gable ridge running along z so the roof faces point front and back. I'm calculating the roof slope by picking a rise of 0.11 over a half-width of 0.15 plus overhang, giving a pitch angle of about 36.3 degrees.

For the gable itself, I'm extruding a triangular outline (base corners plus the ridge peak) into a prism matching the wall's depth, positioned right at the wall top so it caps the box. Then the roof panels become boxes sized along the slope length, with each panel's width along the ridge extended slightly beyond the depth for overhang.

Still working out the panel positions...

For the roof itself, I'm deciding between a snowy white icing look versus a chocolate wafer base with colorful pastel candy tiles, leaning toward dark brown with peppermint-colored tiles plus snow drifts and icicles along the ridge for visual contrast.

Now I'm laying out the candy tiles as small round discs arranged in staggered rows across each roof panel, calculating their positions along the slope and width with shingle-style offsetting so alternate rows interlock like real roof tiles.

To avoid z-fighting, I'll increase the normal offset for lower rows so they sit higher and visually overlap the rows above, matching real shingle layering. Then I'm adding a ridge cap as a white icing sweep with beads, plus snow drift lumps on the roof surface and icicles along the eave edges.

Along each eave edge I'm placing a white icing rod with hanging cone icicles of varying length and spacing, and I'm also adding barge board trim with scalloped bead dots along the gable edges at the front and back.

Now I'm adding a round peppermint window decoration on the gable, a flat circle facing outward near the roof peak, textured with the peppermint pattern.

For the walls, I'm placing the front door centered at z = D/2, defining its arched outline by computing points along a semicircle for the top curve and extruding it into a door shape.

Since extrusions only support flat paint rather than textures, I'm planning the door as a chocolate-brown extruded body, topped with a white icing arch frame, plus small raised box panels to simulate chocolate bar squares as decoration.

Working out the arch geometry for the door panels, knob, and candy-slab steps, then sketching the white icing door frame as a swept arc path with computed point coordinates.

I'm positioning the front windows away from the candy-cane columns flanking the door, settling on roughly ±0.1 centered placement with a warm glowing window texture that includes brown cross muntins.

Now I'm planning the window details: candy-colored mint shutters, a white sill box, and tiny gumdrop accents, building toward a reusable helper function for placing windows at any position with a given normal direction.

Working through the axis orientation for the +X-facing wall, confirming the viewer's right side matches the plane's local x-axis so textures won't be mirrored. Now moving on to placing windows on the side walls at x=±0.15.

I'm thinking through decoration details for the back wall—likely just a centered window with a small candy wreath to keep it simple—and planning icing details for the base: a bead row around the bottom of the walls plus white corner posts at the four corners for that classic candy-house look, with a trim rod along the top front edge.

Now I'm adding piped icing along the front gable edges with a zigzag/bead pattern, and considering a decorative candy band under the front eaves—a horizontal row of alternating red, green, and white round candies like M&Ms.

I'm also placing a chimney on the right roof slope, computing its position and height so it sits on the slanted surface and pokes above the ridge, factoring in the roof's slope to figure out where its base and top should land.

I'll build a custom brick pattern paint with offset rows and white mortar lines, then top the chimney with a lumpy white icing cap and stack flattened pink-and-white spheres above it as cotton-candy smoke puffs. I'm also adding white icing drifts as flattened spheres along the roof ridge and slopes near the chimney for a snowy effect.

Now I'm scattering a few extra snow lumps at random positions across each roof panel, keeping them near the edges so the tiles stay visible, and designing the base board as a gold-foil box with a rope-like icing border around its edge.

For the snow mound covering the board, I'm extruding a rounded rectangular outline with bevel smoothing to get a soft, flattened icing shape rather than a plain box.

I'm working out the vertical placement: snow spans roughly 0.019 to 0.035 to sit above the board (0 to 0.02), and the house walls will start around 0.032-0.034 so they appear slightly nestled into the snow.

For the snow material, I'm mottling white with a pale blue to suggest soft shadowing, and I'll scatter some drift-like flattened sphere lumps near the house base and trees for texture. For the gumdrop decorations, I'm building a hemisphere helper (open-bottom sphere geometry, squashed slightly on the y-axis) that sits just at the snow surface, with flat sugary coloring.

Now I'm figuring out the speckle paint approach, calculating texel density so the sugar-coating noise reads at roughly 1.4mm resolution, and bumping paint resolution up to 2048 for crisper detail. Then I'm sketching out the tree design as stacked frosted cones in decreasing sizes, trimmed with scalloped icing, sugar-pearl rings, and a yellow star topper.

I'm shifting to a lathe-based tree profile instead of plain cones, building a faceted scalloped silhouette per tier and placing rings of alternating-colored candy balls at each tier edge, plus positioning a few trees at scattered coordinates across the scene.

For lollipops, I'm designing a thin white stick topped with a textured disc — using back-to-back circles or a thin cylinder with radial UV mapping so the candy-swirl texture shows properly on both faces.

I'm planning the lollipop texture variations with cached SVG patterns, then sketching candy canes as curved paths—straight stems with a hooked arc at the top using control points for the semicircle bend.

I'm thinking about caching the paint function per cane using an approximate path length, but worrying that with 8 sides the angular seam from 315° back to 0° could cause an interpolation smear in the stripe pattern across one quad—likely a minor visual artifact, so I'll accept it and consider alternatives.

I'm also planning out where candy canes get used decoratively: flanking the door as straight striped pillars with gumdrop caps, and lined up along the front garden as fence posts with hooks.

I'll add stepping stones along the path from the door to the fence gap, then sketch the gingerbread man as an outline shape: a rounded octagon head on a simple body, defined with small-scale coordinates so the proportions stay convincing at this size.

Still plotting coordinates...

I'll keep smoothing at 1 and scale everything down to meters, giving the figure a height around 0.08. For the face, I'm planning tiny icing dot eyes, a smile sweep, three gumdrop buttons down the chest, and white zigzag piping at the wrists and ankles, then positioning the figure standing upright on the snow with its feet resting at the base height.

Now I'm working out the orientation so the gingerbread man can stand propped at a slight angle facing the door, computing the thickness axis as the cross product of the tilted x-direction and the y-axis to get the correct facing normal, settling on roughly a -20° rotation.

Then I'm figuring out how to place detail points using the extruded Part's local coordinate frame, checking whether the local() mapping takes raw numeric arrays scaled against the outline's own axes, and confirming the frame's origin aligns with the drawing's placement point.

To avoid depending on the API's exact behavior, I decide to write my own placement helper instead -- defining a simple plane struct with origin, x/y axes, and normal, then computing points as origin plus offsets along each axis. This gives me direct control for positioning things like a chimney or sphere.

Now I'm thinking through the wall coloring, planning a mottled gingerbread texture with varying brown shades and some weathering effects.

I'm writing a custom paint function that layers noise-based color blending for the base gingerbread tone, adds darker speckles using a cell pattern for spice specks, and lightens the top-facing surfaces for a baked look, while double-checking that functions like `cells`, `mix`, and `smoothstep` are properly exported from the SDK.

Walls and gable prisms will reuse this same gingerbread paint, and I'm deciding to skip adding icing dust at the wall base to keep things simple. Now I'm setting up a separate white icing material for later use.

Still defining color palette...

Thinking about limiting sugar paint to gumdrops rather than tiles, keeping tile discs flat-colored without extra gloss, and working out the painted-area budget—board getting flat gold while snow and other painted surfaces need density calculations based on canvas resolution.

Checking that texel density at 2048px gives roughly 1700 texels/m, which comfortably resolves 3mm speckle detail. Triangle counts seem manageable, and I'm deciding which elements glow—windows and the star topper yes, peppermints no—before starting to write the actual import statements and builder setup code.

Setting up constants and helper functions...

Writing rounded-rectangle geometry...

Adding the extrusion bevel settings, then sweeping a thin rope along the board's edge path using a closed catmull curve, and scattering alternating pink and white candy dots along that rope using positional frames from the path.

For the walls I'm sizing the box around the gable area, then handling the gable extrusion so its bottom face sits flush with the wall top without z-fighting, matching thickness exactly to the depth. Now I'm moving on to the roof pan geometry.
